rv.q: But the shaggy script is in desperate need of trimming and shaping, while Thomas Caruso’s production is so stiff that a reading might have succeeded better than a full staging.
Enormously entertaining, Caroline Aaron, Brooke Adams, Marilu Henner and Melanie Mayron are great company and great fun to be around.

As contrived as it is, Madwomen of the West still fascinates with its unapologetic and humorous depiction of older women and their grievances, and would make an ideal post-brunch activity for you and your close circle of friends.
More importantly, it provides a superb showcase for four actresses we don't see enough of on stage.
During this “girl-talk” affair, however, more than seems helpful comes across as forced.
But anyone looking for a smart contemporary comedy should, in the words of Dionne Warwick, walk on by.

It is ironic that a production so fueled by feminist power thus falls prey to two qualities that are anathema to the cause: an overeagerness to please and insecurity over how best to get its message across.

cn.t: This boomer-targeted comedy about aging women at a birthday brunch draws mixed reviews. Critics praise the charismatic cast but find the script unfocused, rambling through cultural grievances and dated jokes with uneven results.
